The kinds of stories we tell
How thoughts and state reinforce each other

sections.title: An example: an argument with your spouse
How it takes away your power

blocks.p: This is the first in a series on what keeps you stuck. This one is about your stories.

There are different kinds of stories. Some are just things that pop into your mind: explanations, memories, images. To me, those count as stories. But here I want to focus on the conscious thoughts in our minds. The words in our mind, the beliefs.

blocks.h: Why changing your thoughts is so hard

blocks.p: Usually, when we talk about thoughts, we talk about thought replacement. In my field, at least in the more medical model of therapy, like county mental health and the government and nonprofit level, the idea is that if we can just change the way people think, their behavior problems or their symptoms will ease.

There might be some truth in that. I don't think it's without value. But to me, that's always been a very slow and clumsy way of making change. It's really hard to just switch up your thoughts. "Just stop thinking that way." "You've got to think more positively." "You've got to find more gratitude." There might be some value in that, but it's not the answer. Just changing your thoughts, in my opinion, isn't super helpful, unless you can actually do it.
The problem is that our thoughts aren't there on their own. They come from our polyvagal state. This is the concept of story follows state.

The state of our autonomic nervous system dictates the flavor of our thoughts. Each of us has our own unique, individual, wonderful thoughts, but their flavor follows the tone of our autonomic nervous system.

ul: Safe and social state: your thoughts will be empathetic and understanding. You'll be motivated, with belief in yourself and in other people. You'll see the good in people, and you'll generally think more positively.
Flight or fight: in more of an anxious energy, or a fight state, your thoughts will be based more around fear and identifying danger, blame, and avoiding responsibility.
Shutdown: your thoughts will be more about how worthless or pointless things are.

blocks.p: So your thoughts come from the state of your autonomic nervous system. Addressing the thoughts can be helpful, but what we're really talking about is addressing the state of your whole body: how prepared for safety or danger you are. Your thoughts might not be the primary issue. Your state, in my opinion, is the primary issue.

blocks.h: The kinds of stories we tell

blocks.p: Even within these word-type stories, there are different kinds.

Your value and worth. You might have stories about how worthless you are, or maybe how great you are. These can be polar extremes, depending on what state you're in and how intense it is. Both have pitfalls, and neither is probably true. Stories don't have to be true, and in a lot of cases I think they're just flat-out wrong. But not always.

The thing that happened. "It's my fault that..." "I shouldn't have..." "If I didn't do this, then that wouldn't have happened." "If I was a better kid, then my parents would have..." Fill in the blank. I can't tell you what that is for you. Your brain is trying to explain what's happening within you, your state, in the context of the thing that happened, or maybe the things that didn't happen.
Blame or avoidance. "I'm like this because of you." "I'm like this because of some context, whatever it is."

The possibility of change. I might say, "You can do it. You can make change in your life." If you're in a shutdown state, you'll go to, "No. Somebody else can. That doesn't apply to me." Your stories about the possibility of change shift based on the state you're in.

Story follows state is a very integral part of Polyvagal Theory. And to me, it's not just knowledge. It's foundational. If you can learn this, the amount of self-judgment and self-blame you carry can go down.

Every time someone learns this, my clients in therapy or people who write to me, they say something like, "I learned Polyvagal Theory, I learned story follows state, I learned these different pieces, and it's normalizing. It makes sense." Having that top-down new story, a new narrative for who you are and how you are, can really reduce the intensity of your stuck defensive state. And I think all of us have some stuck defensive state.

blocks.h: How thoughts and state reinforce each other

blocks.p: Here's how this connects to Polyvagal Theory. The thoughts in our mind come from the state we're in. But those thoughts also communicate with the brainstem, and the body communicates with the brainstem too. We say body to brain and brain to body, but if you want to take it to the next level, it's top brain to brainstem, and body to brainstem. The brainstem is where the really primitive, neuroception-level stuff happens, and where the bodily shifts take place.

So the words in our brain send a signal to our body, and the pass-through is the brainstem. Top-down thoughts are a cue of safety or danger, and that affects what polyvagal state we're in. Changing our thoughts could be helpful, but it's really hard to start there. Usually, when you change your state, your thoughts change along with it.

You can also do self-regulation from the body up to the brainstem. You can feel into your stuck defensive state mindfully, and then do something: it could be something creative, singing, a deep breath, pushing against the wall. Whatever you need in that moment. That can send signals of release, discharge, or safety to your brainstem.

But your thoughts send signals to your brainstem too, and when you're coming from a defensive state, the thoughts end up reinforcing the state you're in. They come from your polyvagal state, and they also reinforce it. Being in the state brings the thoughts, story follows state, and then the thoughts reinforce the state. It's a very frustrating cycle, and it keeps you stuck.

blocks.h3: An example: an argument with your spouse

blocks.p: Say you're in a fight state, in an argument with your spouse. From a fight state, the thought will be, "It's my spouse's fault we're in an argument. It's not about me, it's about them. They're terrible, and it's their fault I feel this way."

You can see how the thought comes from the angry fight state you're already in, and then it sends cues back down to the body: "Yeah, you're right to be tense. You're right to be heated, because it is their fault. There is a danger." That's the feedback loop, brain to body and body to brain, through the brainstem.

blocks.h3: How it takes away your power

blocks.p: That loop can also take away your responsibility, your role in the situation. Your thoughts keep you stuck in the cycle, and they also absolve you of being part of the solution. If it's the other person's fault, it's up to them to find the solution, right? I think everybody's responsible for their part in their life, and this takes away the responsibility to shift your own behavior and your own state.

It actually gives power to the other person. If your wellbeing depends on somebody else, that gives them a lot of power. If it's their fault you feel the way you feel, then in your mind it might be up to them to get you out of that feeling. That's way too much power, and it keeps you stuck.
Of course, two spouses, two friends, whoever it is, we all bear responsibility. We all have to do our part in making change. But we don't control other people, so it ultimately starts with us.
The solution is to actually feel into your stuck defensive state, whether it's flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, as much as you can. It's not easy. Not easy.

But feel into it mindfully. And not just the defensive stuff. Also feel the safety, the capacity for safety, because it is there. Maybe it's hard to access. Maybe it's hard to feel. Maybe it's hard to identify what safety even feels like in the first place. But I believe we all have some access to it.
Feeling safety comes first and foremost. We have to have that as a foundation, and this top-down learning is part of that. So:

ol: Identify what brings your body to safety.
Then, as you're ready, feel into that stuck defensive state.

blocks.p: That's what will help change your thoughts, your stories. Just addressing the stories can be helpful, but it's a big challenge.
That said, a reframe can absolutely be helpful. Giving someone a new way of looking at things can land as, "Oh, I never thought about it that way."

That's not saying, "Hey, think differently," or, "Hey, be more appreciative." In therapy, if someone's open to hearing it, I might say, "The way I'm hearing it is this," and it flips things to a different angle. That can be a top-down cue of safety. It's another way of looking at a situation, one that probably doesn't come from a defensive state.

For example, a child's tantrum can be viewed as an annoyance. It can be viewed as the kid being manipulative. Or it can be viewed as a child communicating a need. I'm not saying any of these is right or wrong. But one of them carries a lot less judgment and blame, and probably opens more avenues for change, connection, and building the relationship.
Another reframe, and this has a lot to do with the name Stuck Not Broken: if someone believes, "I am broken and unfixable," that can be reframed as, "I'm stuck, and I'm learning how to get unstuck."
Both are beliefs about the possibility of change. But one is a lot more blaming and reinforces the stuck defensive state, and the other is more of an avenue for hope and for change.
